query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The high thermal and chemical stability of laser-synthesized HEA nanoparticles is governed by the formation of defective graphene shells during laser irradiation, which encapsulate the nanoparticles and strongly anchor them to the LIG substrate, thereby inhibiting coalescence and elemental segregation under high-temperature service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A dried film of mixed metal precursors uniformly adsorbed on a 3D porous, edge-rich laser-induced graphene (LIG) substrate.
generation.intervention: Laser irradiation of the precursor-coated LIG to induce both thermal decomposition of precursors and in situ formation of defective, encapsulating graphene shells; compare this with nanoparticles synthesized on a non-porous, smooth carbon substrate.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regimes relevant to catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K) where nanoparticles are prone to sintering and phase segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Graphene shell encapsulation with abundant defective edge planes from the LIG substrate.
generation.mechanism: Laser irradiation generates rapid localized heating that drives precursor thermal decomposition and metal reduction via thermionic emission, forming molten HEA nanoparticles. Simultaneously, the high temperature induces bending of surrounding graphene layers, which develop defects and encapsulate the nanoparticles. This encapsulation enhances binding energy and provides a physical barrier that prevents nanoparticle coalescence and elemental segregation at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles synthesized on LIG with graphene encapsulation will exhibit reduced sintering and maintain a more uniform elemental distribution under high-temperature conditions compared to nanoparticles synthesized on smooth carbon supports that lack such encapsulation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced on non-porous carbon substrates without the formation of a graphene shell, which are expected to show greater agglomeration and phase segregation when subjected to high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is predicted to be effective primarily for HEA nanoparticles synthesized via the laser solid-phase method on porous, edge-rich LIG. Alternative synthesis routes or supports with different surface properties may not exhibit the same degree of stabilization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative advantage in thermal and chemical stability conferred by the graphene shell encapsulation remains uncertain and may vary with differences in HEA composition, laser parameters, and service environment.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of HEA nanoparticles: one using laser irradiation on LIG to produce graphene-encapsulated nanoparticles, and a control group using the same laser parameters on a smooth, non-porous carbon substrate that does not facilitate graphene shell formation. Expose both groups to service regimes spanning 773–1173 K (for catalytic conditions) and 473–1923 K (for thermoelectric conditions).
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to assess nanoparticle size distribution and detect agglomeration.
Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) to evaluate elemental homogeneity and segregation.
X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase stability and crystallographic integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the graphene-encapsulated nanoparticles and the control nanoparticles on smooth carbon exhibit similar degrees of structural integrity, agglomeration, and elemental distribution after high-temperature treatment, then the protective role of the graphene shell in stabilizing HEA nanoparticles is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) offers new opportunities to develop functional materials in widespread applications. Although some methods have successfully produced HEA NPs, these methods generally require rigorous conditions such as high pressure, high temperature, restricted atmosphere, and limited substrates, which impede practical viability. In this work, we report laser solid-phase synthesis of CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles by laser irradiation of mixed metal precursors on a laser-induced graphene (LIG) support with a 3D porous structure. The CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles are embraced by several graphene layers, forming graphene shell-encapsulated HEA nanoparticles. The mechanisms of the laser solid-phase synthesis of HEA NPs on LIG supports are investigated through theoretical simulation and experimental observations, in consideration of mixed metal precursor adsorption, thermal decomposition, reduction through electrons from laser-induced thermionic emission, and liquid beads splitting. The production rate reaches up to 30 g/h under the current laser setup. The laser-synthesized graphene shell-encapsulated CrMnFeCoNi NPs loaded on LIG-coated carb

We intended to gain an understanding of the HEA NP formation through thermodynamic modeling and experimental measurements in terms of temperature variation and electron emission under laser irradiation, to provide a theoretical basis and a reliable technical route for the rapid laser synthesis of HEA NPs. We chose CrMnFeCoNi, as CrMnFeCoNi is relatively a well-researched alloy among the HEAs, in which both miscible (Cr/Fe) and immiscible metal pairs (Mn/Co) are present. We used the laser-induced 3D porous graphene from polybenzimidazole (PBI) to serve as the host to adsorb mixed metal salt precursors and then subjected it to laser irradiation using a Nd:YAG laser with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a pulse width of 30 ns. The effects of laser fluences and concentrations of the mixed metal precursors on the size of HEA NPs were investigated. We studied the synthesis mechanism through laser-induced photothermal decomposition of the metal precursors in combination with laser-induced thermionic emission reduction. Compared with the laser ablation in liquid, laser solid-phase synthesis offers a new route of HEA NP synthesis which can be characterized by fine controllability, no post-treatm

As described above, during laser irradiation, the conversion of the HEA NPs from the mixed metal precursors adsorbed on LIG involves several processes, including thermal decomposition, metal ion reduction, metallic element melting, molten bead fusion, and fission, depending on the temperature experience. The laser synthesis in this work is based on solid-phase, which is different from liquid-phase synthesis. As the mixed metal precursor is adsorbed on the 3D porous LIG structure and dried before laser irradiation, the size of the nanoparticles can be well controlled by the laser fluence, and the concentration of the precursor due to the limited mobility of the reduced metal species and subsequently the nanoparticles.

The laser-synthesized CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles are embraced by several graphene layers, forming graphene shell-encapsulated nanoparticles. This might be caused by the bending of graphene layers subjected to laser heating, which was also reported in the work on graphene nanosphere formation by microwave heating. Embracing the metal nanoparticles by graphene layers is beneficial to the dispersion of the nanoparticles by preventing nanoparticles from aggregation. On the other hand, the analysis of the LIG indicates that the LIG is characterized by a high density of edge planes (Fig. S4c, Supporting Information), which are highly defective, offering preferred sites to immobilize the HEA nanoparticles (Fig. S4d, Supporting Information). This phenomenon was also reported in the synthesis of metallic nanoparticles on carbon supports through the Joule heating method. Both characteristics of the laser-synthesized CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles on LIG support described above offer a reinforced effect on the nanoparticles with strong adhesion to the LIG, which might contribute to the high stability of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles catalysts in catalytic applications.

The electrocatalytic performance described in this work is superior to most of the non-precious HEA catalysts reported up to date. Particularly, the stability of the laser-synthesized IE-HEA/LIG outperforms most of the precious and non-precious HEA catalysts. This might be explained in consideration of the following aspects. Firstly, the laser-synthesized CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles are the form of the graphene shell-encapsulated. This hybrid structure offers benefits for enhancing the electronic transport from the LIG to the active sites, and the incomplete wrap (Fig. 1f and Fig. S4a, b) benefits the exposure of the HEA NPs active sites, lowering the barrier of electrons transfer in electrolysis. During the OER performance, the physical constraint effect also prevents nanoparticles from aggregating and peeling off from the LIG support under the harsh working environment, thus enhancing the durability of the catalyst. On the other hand, the carbon shell directly acts as an active site due to the electronic structure modulated by the core metal NP, which is beyond the scope of this paper.
